chunks: And ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī ʿAbd Allāh said to al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام:
I feel wind in my stomach until I think that it has come out.
So he said: “There is no wudu (ablution) upon you until you hear the sound or perceive the wind.”
Then he said: “Indeed, Iblis sits between the buttocks of a man and causes an occurrence so as to make him doubt.”

key_terms.إِبْلِيسَ: Iblis, Satan, who seeks to cast doubt and confusion
key_terms.الرِّيحَ: wind; here, passing wind that may nullify wudu (ablution)
key_terms.الصَّوْتَ: an audible sound indicating certainty of passing wind
key_terms.لِيُشَكِّكَهُ: to make him doubt or fall into uncertainty
key_terms.وُضُوءٌ: wudu (ablution), the ritual state of purity required for worship

ai.seo_question: Does doubt about passing wind break wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling regarding doubt in nullification of wudu (ablution): mere suspicion that wind may have exited does not invalidate ritual purity. Certainty is established only by clear indication, and the hadith also warns that such intrusive doubt can be a means by which Iblis troubles a person in worship.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.139 - Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdullah asked Imam Jafar ibn Muhammad Al-Sadiq (as) said:
'I feel wind in my stomach to the extent that I think it has exited.'
Imam (as) said: 'You do not need to perform ablution unless you hear a sound or perceive the smell.'

Imam (as) then added:
'Indeed, Satan sits between a man's buttocks and causes him to think he has passed wind to make him doubt.'.
